title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Mason County starts construction today while Kalamazoo, Garfield Twp and others hit pause.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Saturday night, and our big story tonight is the groundbreaking in Mason County on two new large-scale data centers.
Right, and that comes just as several other townships are hitting the brakes. Let's start there.
Western Mason County approved construction today. The projects will pull a lot of power from the regional grid and bring construction and operations jobs.
But locals are already talking about what it means for power reliability and tax revenue. How did we get here so fast?
This fits a pattern we've seen building all year. AI demand is driving proposals across the state, and utilities are looking at big load growth.
Right, and that raises the usual questions about who pays for upgrades and whether bills go up for everyone else.
Exactly. Data centers can use as much power as a small city, so when they come online the grid has to handle it.
And water use is another big one, especially in places already watching aquifer levels.
Mason County residents will feel the tax side too. New facilities often mean new revenue, but it depends on how the deals are structured.
So is this the first major project to actually break ground this month, or have others moved forward quietly?
It's one of the first visible groundbreakings we've tracked in western Michigan. Most of the action lately has been in zoning fights and moratoriums.
That tracks with what we saw yesterday in Kalamazoo, where they added a moratorium to slow things down.
Yes, and Garfield Township in Grand Traverse County is taking a full year to write rules on power demand, noise, and water.
That delay gives residents time to weigh the trade-offs before anything advances. Smart move or just kicking the can?
It buys breathing room. A lot of these townships are small and don't have dedicated staff for complex utility issues.
Meanwhile, a university town hall yesterday gave Mid-Michigan residents their first concrete numbers on megawatts and daily water use.
That's the kind of detail people need when projects are proposed within 30 miles.
And over on the Lakeshore, one township is already using existing zoning to block data centers near homes and wells.
Nearby towns are watching to see if the same language works for them.
Then there's the planned protest today in the Ypsilanti area over water use at two proposed campuses.
Activists say those could draw millions of gallons daily. Homeowners in Washtenaw and Wayne counties have a stake.
A farm owner on Friday pushed for city annexation to build on rural land, shifting taxes and control.
That move would change land use and services for residents 30 miles away if it succeeds.
And the University of Michigan computing center plans drew questions on Friday about possible nuclear weapons ties.
Ann Arbor residents want clearer answers on how the project could support military programs.
In Lenox Township on Thursday, residents demanded full disclosure after learning about proposals through back channels.
The worry there is noise, power strain, and lost farmland in Macomb County.
Also Thursday, a second recall bid failed for an official tied to a data center rezoning.
Voters are watching how these fights shape future development across the region.
Back to Mason County though. What happens next now that shovels are in the ground?
Construction jobs start immediately, but the real test will be when the facilities come online and start drawing power.
And whether the promised tax revenue actually offsets any rate impacts for everyone else.
Utilities will be watching closely. These projects often require grid upgrades that get socialized.
Right, and farmland conversion is permanent once the concrete is poured.
That's why so many townships are writing new rules before more proposals land.
How many have paused or are studying impacts now?
At least a handful across the state, from Kalamazoo to Grand Traverse and west Michigan.
It feels like a statewide recalibration after the initial rush.
Residents are asking the same questions everywhere: power bills, water, noise, and who benefits.
And whether local boards have enough information before approving anything.
The Mason projects will be a live test case for the rest of the state.
We'll be tracking how the grid handles the new load and what the first bills look like.
Exactly. Moving to quick hits now.
Kalamazoo added a moratorium yesterday to slow the rush while they study impacts.
Residents there could see fewer projects competing for power and land in the short term.
Garfield Township is spending a full year drafting rules on zoning and permitting.
That gives locals time to weigh taxes, traffic, and grid effects before anything advances.
A university town hall yesterday laid out power and water demands for Mid-Michigan residents.
People within 30 miles got concrete numbers on megawatts and daily use.
Lakeshore township blocked data centers using existing zoning rules near homes and wells.
Nearby west Michigan towns are watching to see if the same approach works.
Ypsilanti-area residents plan a protest today over water use at two proposed campuses.
The Saturday event targets projects that could draw millions of gallons daily.
A farm is seeking city annexation to build a data center on Friday's news.
That would shift tax revenue and local control away from the township.
University of Michigan plans for a new computing center raised nuclear weapons worries on Friday.
Ann Arbor residents and activists want clearer answers on military program ties.
Lenox Township residents demanded answers on hidden data center plans on Thursday.
The push comes amid worries about noise, power strain, and lost farmland in Macomb County.
A second recall bid failed Thursday for an official tied to data center rezoning.
The fight centers on land-use changes that could open the door to more server farms.
On deck for listeners who want to attend something in person.
The Ypsilanti-area protest is happening today at the Van Buren Township line.
It's a direct action on water use concerns for those two proposed campuses.
Next week several townships are expected to continue work on their new zoning rules.
Garfield Township's year-long process is just getting started, so check local notices.
And the Mid-Michigan university town hall series may have follow-ups.
Always verify dates and times on your township website.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Mason County Breaks Ground on Data Centers as Townships Push Back Statewide
